title: The Covered Wagon
byline: Dir. James Cruze; Famous Players-Lasky (Paramount), 1923. Based on the novel by Emerson Hough (1922).

evidence.note: US work published 1923; 95-year maximum copyright term expired January 1, 2019. All US works from 1923 entered the public domain on that date regardless of renewal status.
evidence.source: Cornell Copyright Information Center — Copyright Term and the Public Domain in the United States

evidence.note: Silent film — no original recorded score exists. The Archive.org item (identifier: the-covered-wagon-1923-by-james-cruze) is a 1080p Blu-ray rip carrying an added AAC audio track. That modern musical accompaniment is a separately authored, independently protected work. The photographic images are public domain; any modern score on a commercial copy is not.

Adapted from Emerson Hough's novel 'The Covered Wagon,' first published in book form in 1922 by D. Appleton & Co. (serialized in the Saturday Evening Post, 1922). As a US work published in 1922, its 95-year copyright term expired January 1, 2018. Both the source novel and the film adaptation are public domain by term.
evidence.source: Cornell Copyright Information Center — Copyright Term and the Public Domain in the United States

evidence.note: A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright: copying or restoring public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). What a restoration ADDS can be protected: a newly composed or newly recorded score, colorization, newly written or translated titles and subtitles, and other original additions. Separately, ripping a copy-protected Blu-ray or DVD can break the DMCA's anti-circumvention rule (17 U.S.C. 1201) even when the film itself is public domain.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp. (summary)

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. 1201 - circumvention of copyright protection systems.

A modern 1080p Blu-ray edition is confirmed by the file manifest in the Archive.org item: filename 'The.Covered.Wagon.1923.1080p.BluRay.x264.AAC-[YTS.MX].mp4' establishes a commercial Blu-ray source. Kino Lorber has released this title on home video with a new restoration and added musical score. The restoration print and its commissioned score are new copyrightable works separate from the PD original.

editorial:
The Covered Wagon (1923) is the film that created the template for the Hollywood epic Western. Directed by James Cruze for Famous Players-Lasky — the corporation that became Paramount Pictures — it stars J. Warren Kerrigan, Lois Wilson, and Ernest Torrence in a dramatization of the 1848 Oregon Trail emigration. Cruze filmed on location in Utah's Millard County desert with a production that assembled roughly 500 wagons and 3,000 extras; the scale was unprecedented. The film grossed an estimated $4 million against an $800,000 budget, becoming one of the top commercial performers of the decade. For contemporary creators it offers extensive authentic footage of covered-wagon caravans, river crossings, large cavalry engagements, and frontier camp life that would cost many millions to recreate — all drawn from the public-domain 1923 print.

The rights trap here is the audio track. The Covered Wagon was a silent film and has no original recorded score, but every commercial copy in wide circulation — including the 1080p Blu-ray rip hosted on Archive.org — carries a modern musical score composed and recorded after the film's own copyright expired. That score is an independent, protected work. A creator who downloads the Archive.org item and uses it with the audio intact is distributing an unlicensed score. The correct path is to strip the audio track before reuse, or to pair the silent images with music that is itself public domain or explicitly licensed. Kino Lorber's restoration scan adds no new copyright over the underlying images — a faithful reproduction of a public-domain film creates no protectable authorship — but ripping a copy-protected Kino disc can still trigger DMCA anti-circumvention liability, so sourcing from a pre-restoration print removes that exposure entirely.
faq: Can I cut footage from this film into my documentary or commercial project?

Yes — the 1923 photographic images are public domain in the United States and carry no copyright restriction. The critical step is to strip any modern audio track before use. Commercial copies, including the Archive.org item, carry a modern score that is not public domain. Use the silent images only, or pair them with separately cleared music.
Does the Kino Lorber restoration create a new copyright over the film?

No — a faithful digital scan of a public-domain film, including noise reduction and grading, adds no new copyright under U.S. law; those restored images are as free as the 1923 original. The risk is not copyright but the DMCA: ripping a copy-protected Kino Lorber disc to access the restored footage can violate the anti-circumvention rules even though the film itself is public domain. Sourcing from an unprotected print avoids that issue entirely.
